prompt_text:
The figure summarizes several strategies for inducing antigen-specific immune tolerance, mainly in T cells. On the left, tolerizing material such as peptides, full protein, DNA plasmids, mRNA, myelin-reactive T cells, exosomes, or antigen-coupled blood cells is delivered through blood or by tolerogenic dendritic cells and related antigen-presenting cells. These approaches present antigen in a noninflammatory context, illustrated here with myelin-associated targets such as MBP and MOG, to retrain rather than activate immunity.

The central mechanism is that a tolerogenic APC presents peptide–HLA to a T cell and then drives one of several suppressive outcomes. The figure highlights induction of regulatory T cells, release of anti-inflammatory cytokines causing bystander suppression, stimulation without costimulation leading to anergy, and FAS/FASL-mediated apoptosis.

The lower half broadens this concept into therapeutic platforms. One route is engineered cell therapy, where T cells from peripheral or umbilical cord blood are expanded, gene-edited, and equipped with receptors or safety modules before reinfusion. Other routes modulate immune checkpoints such as PD1, CTLA4, and TIM3, or alter broader tolerance pathways in the gut and myeloid compartment, affecting Treg induction, anergy, and deletion. A final panel suggests parasite-based immunomodulation, with Trichuris suis shown as an example.
